title: Scope and Rules of Engagement
summary: Scope and rules of engagement are the written boundary that defines what may be tested, when, how, by whom, and what happens when something goes wrong; without documented authorisation from someone entitled to give it, the same activity is simply unauthorised access. A workable document names in-scope assets precisely enough to be unambiguous, lists excluded systems and data categories, and states testing windows with time zones. It defines permitted and prohibited techniques, for example whether denial-of-service testing, social engineering, physical entry or third-party hosted services are allowed, and it records the source addresses that defenders may allow-list. It sets escalation rules: emergency contacts on both sides, stop conditions such as discovery of an unrelated active intrusion or unexpected service degradation, and the obligation to report critical findings immediately rather than at the final readout. It also covers handling of sensitive data encountered during testing, evidence retention and destruction, deconfliction with the security operations centre, and the treatment of cloud or outsourced services where the provider may require separate notification under a shared responsibility model. Practically, the document protects the tester, the client and the defenders: it reduces false positives because the security operations centre knows when legitimate testing is scheduled, gives a tested route for stopping work, and provides the audit trail that regulators and insurers request. Scope should be reviewed whenever the environment changes materially.
objectives: You will be able to draft a scope section that names in-scope and excluded assets unambiguously.
You will be able to list the technique categories that must be explicitly permitted or prohibited in an engagement.
You will be able to define escalation paths, stop conditions and emergency contacts for a test.
You will be able to explain how deconfliction with a security operations centre reduces false positives.
You will be able to describe the authorisation needed for cloud and third-party hosted services.
You will be able to specify evidence handling, retention and data destruction requirements.
